text: A boy pool hustler with a brother in prison for murder walks into a place that refuses to call him a criminal. Boys Town is a detention facility only on paper; the priest who runs it treats the residents as people responsible for their own improvement. The film spends its ninety-six minutes testing that method against someone who has no interest in being improved and no reason to trust the offer. Whitey Marsh arrives with a thief's reflexes and a grievance he cannot name. He needs Father Flanagan to fail, because failure would confirm that his brother's road was the only one open. The Academy's acting prize went here, and the reason is plain: the argument rests on one man's patience, held steady while a boy keeps raising the price of it.

The Spanish is Mexican, the production is French, and the house at the center stands in countryside its owners were not raised in. Carlos Reygadas builds the film around a family that has moved out to land it can live on without being able to claim, close enough to the people who work that land to hear them. He declines to arbitrate. The countryside is not offered as a refuge. Nothing in a hundred and fifteen minutes settles whether the two worlds complete each other or are slowly at work on each other's elimination, and that unsettled state is not a withheld answer — it is the condition the household wakes into each morning. What arrives in place of explanation is weather, rooms, children, and long stretches in which a family is simply visible.

A boarder takes the spare room in a marriage that had been managing, barely, with no one else in the house. Daniel Mann keeps the picture at that scale — kitchen, staircase, front room, the hours between a husband going out and coming back — so the disturbance has nowhere to go except through the people already there. The young woman does little but be present and be young. That is enough. What had been endurable while unobserved becomes something both spouses can watch themselves doing, and ninety-six minutes is exactly long enough for a routine to stop working without anyone raising a voice. The Academy's award for lead actress went here, which points at where the weight sits: not on the husband's interest but on the wife, and on what a day looks like once its shape has been removed.

No debt, no deal, no ambition: what puts this household in front of a cartel is something a twelve-year-old did without any idea of its size. Amat Escalante, whose direction here took the Ariel, films what follows at ordinary speed — work, the road home, a child to be fed — so that brutality arrives as an interruption of chores rather than as the event the story has been building toward. Heli's difficulty is not survival in the abstract. It is that he has a young family, a sister, and no leverage of any kind, and that the police who might intervene draw from the same well as the men he is hiding from. A hundred and five minutes is not enough time to fix that. The film is not organized around fixing it.

A screenplay about the sitting prime minister reaches the state broadcaster, and the state broadcaster declines. The man carrying it is Bruno Bonomo, who turned out cheap genre pictures in the seventies and has produced nothing for a long while since; the one project that might restore him is the one no institution wants its name on. Nanni Moretti makes his comedy from the mechanics — the pitching, the polite obstruction, the business of assembling a film that keeps not getting assembled. It took the David di Donatello as best film, a domestic judgment on a picture about a subject Italian television would not carry. Berlusconi is named in the premise. What the hundred and twelve minutes actually follow is everyone downstream of him, trying to get work done.

The upper floor of the palazzo was not for rent until a marchesa decided otherwise. Luchino Visconti, whose picture took the David di Donatello as best film, keeps nearly all of it inside that one building: below, a retired professor of American origin who has arranged a life in which nothing arrives unannounced; above, a woman with a lover, a daughter, and the daughter's young man, none of whom treat a closed door as an argument. The professor is not persecuted. He is included, which is harder to refuse. Two hours pass on staircases and in rooms, and the pressure is entirely a matter of access — who may come down, what may be asked, how much of a routine survives other people knowing its schedule.

The business of the realm happens somewhere off screen; what the camera stays for is the marriages. Who is being wed, who is being replaced, what a king does with an afternoon — Alexander Korda's 1932 production lets that succession supply the structure a history film would ordinarily take from politics. The German-born Anne of Cleves arrives as a negotiation and leaves as one, within months. Henry is written large and played larger, and the Academy's acting prize went to that performance: a monarch rendered as appetite and vanity, watched by everyone in the room. Nothing here is monumental. Ninety-seven minutes at the scale of a difficult household, moving at the speed of one.

The Indochina war returned a man to civilian France without the equipment for civilian life, and the film gives him exactly one companion: an orphaned girl with a single free afternoon each week. Sundays are the whole of their friendship. Serge Bourguignon spends a hundred and ten minutes inside that narrow allowance — the walk, the talk, the promises made by two people with nowhere else to be — while the pressure gathers outside the pair, among adults who see a grown man with a child and reach the conclusion available to them. He is not what they think. He is also not well, and the picture is honest that the two facts do not cancel. It carried the Academy's foreign-language award; what earned it is smaller than a prize, an afternoon a week defended by people who cannot explain it.

Two hundred and twenty minutes, and almost nothing in them is an event. In 1935 the regime removes a painter with a medical degree from his own life and sets him down in a village near Eboli, where the sentence is not prison but distance: he may not leave, and there is nowhere to go. Francesco Rosi lets the confinement set the pace. Days are long, visits are few, the training he set aside for painting turns useful in a place with fewer options, and the village's own arrangements — work, weather, illness, who is owed what — do not reorganize themselves for his benefit. What alters is the exile's estimate of where he has landed. The BAFTA for a film not in English went to it, and it earns its length by refusing to compress a year that was not compressed.

The distance between a salary and an allowance is the whole obstacle in this romance, and the film does not pretend otherwise. Kitty Foyle works for her money; the young man comes from people whose money predates him and who intend to keep the line uncomplicated. Sam Wood stays on her side of that arrangement for a hundred and eight minutes. The family's disapproval never arrives as cruelty — it comes as courtesy, as plans made on her behalf, as the assumption that a sensible girl will see the sense in it. She does see it. That is the trouble. The Academy's award for lead actress went here, and what it recognizes is composure: a woman doing arithmetic in front of people who have never had to do any.

The role is Othello, the wife is playing opposite him, and the stage is the safest place either of them will be that evening. George Cukor's picture opens as a backstage drama and drifts, without a seam, into a thriller: a long run of performances, a marriage that is also a working partnership, and an actor who cannot get a part to stay inside the theatre. The jealousy is borrowed. It is not returned. A hundred and four minutes is a tight frame for a possession this gradual, and the film uses it by keeping the two lives adjacent — dressing room and apartment, rehearsal and dinner — until the vocabulary of one turns up in the other. The Academy's lead acting prize went here, and it had to: everything the film knows has to be legible on one man working in two registers at once.

A body by the water, and a town small enough that the detective will have met most of his suspects before the week is out. Andrea Molaioli gives the case ninety-five minutes — short for a mystery, and the compression shows: no room for a manhunt, only for questions asked one household at a time, and for the answers people give knowing they will see the questioner again tomorrow. The victim is a teenage girl, and the film is careful about what it does with her. What it examines is the community around the case: reputations, old arrangements, the particular silence of neighbours who are also witnesses. Italy's David di Donatello named it best film of its year; the case itself stays small, which is the size the film wants.

Custody is the fight; the ring is only where the money is supposed to come from. King Vidor's 1931 picture runs eighty-six minutes and concerns a prizefighter well past his usefulness — a drinker, unreliable, and without qualification the person his son wants to be with. The film never asks whether the boy is right about him. It asks what will be done about it, since the case against the father is easy to assemble and anyone with standing to bring it will be steadier, better dressed, and more obviously correct. That imbalance is the engine. The Academy's acting prize went here, to a man playing a fighter who cannot land a punch on his own circumstances and keeps presenting himself for the next round.

A man finds a ruined actress at the bottom of her luck and decides she is a project — his house, his money, his fiancée's understanding. Seventy-nine minutes is all Alfred E. Green needs, and the brevity is part of the argument: the decision is made early and the rest is payment. Joyce Heath was a star. She is now someone being managed by a benefactor who has not asked what she wants and would not know what to do with the answer. Don Bellows arranges everything — a stage to put her back on, a fiancée to be released, a Connecticut house to dry out in. The Academy's acting award went to the wreck rather than the rescuer, which is the right reading: the film belongs to the woman being handled, and she understands the arrangement better than the man financing it.
